stimuli.text: Researchers investigated whether a smiling expression makes cartoons seem funnier. They recruited 90 university students and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Participants in one condition held a pen between their teeth, which produces a smile. Participants in the other condition held a pen between their lips, which prevents a smile. The researchers then recorded the rating from 1 to 10 that each participant gave to a set of cartoons.

Researchers investigated whether cognitive-behavioral therapy reduces depression. They recruited 90 adults diagnosed with major depressive disorder and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Participants in one condition received twelve weekly sessions of cognitive-behavioral therapy. Participants in the other condition were placed on a waiting list for twelve weeks and were treated afterward. The researchers then recorded each participant's score on a standard depression questionnaire after twelve weeks.

Researchers investigated whether mindfulness meditation lowers stress. They recruited 84 office workers and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Participants in one condition practiced mindfulness meditation for twenty minutes a day for eight weeks. Participants in the other condition listened to an audiobook for twenty minutes a day for eight weeks. The researchers then recorded the level of the stress hormone cortisol in a saliva sample from each participant.

Researchers collected data from 1,000 students. For each one, they recorded intelligence test score at age 11 and average school grade at age 16. The correlation between the two measures was r = +0.60.

Researchers investigated whether regular aerobic exercise improves memory in older adults. They recruited 100 adults aged 60 to 75 and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Participants in one condition walked briskly for 40 minutes three times a week for six months. Participants in the other condition did gentle stretching for the same amount of time. The researchers then recorded the number of locations that each participant correctly recalled on a spatial memory test.

Researchers investigated whether spreading study sessions out improves long-term retention. They recruited 90 high school students and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Participants in one condition studied a list of 40 words in six ten-minute sessions on six different days. Participants in the other condition studied the same list in a single sixty-minute session. The researchers then recorded the number of words out of 40 that each participant recalled on a test one month later.

Researchers collected data from 300 families. For each one, they recorded the warmth of parenting, as rated by observers and the child's self-esteem score. The correlation between the two measures was r = +0.48.

Researchers investigated whether an expected reward reduces children's later interest in drawing. They recruited 60 preschool children who enjoyed drawing and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Children in one condition were promised a certificate for drawing and received it. Children in the other condition drew with no reward mentioned. The researchers then recorded the number of minutes that each child chose to spend drawing during free time one week later. The results are shown in the table. The difference between the two groups had a p value of 0.01.

rows.group: The group that was promised a certificate
The group that drew without a reward

stimuli.text: Researchers investigated whether a phone conversation reduces what drivers notice. They recruited 64 licensed drivers and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Participants in one condition held a hands-free phone conversation while using a driving simulator. Participants in the other condition used the driving simulator without a phone. The researchers then recorded the number of road signs out of 30 that each participant failed to notice.

Researchers collected data from 600 university students. For each one, they recorded conscientiousness score on a personality inventory and grade point average. The correlation between the two measures was r = +0.35.

Researchers investigated whether caffeine improves attention. They recruited 80 university students and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Participants in one condition drank coffee containing 200 milligrams of caffeine. Participants in the other condition drank decaffeinated coffee that tasted the same. The researchers then recorded the number of targets that each participant correctly detected in a ten-minute computer task. The results are shown in the table. The difference between the two groups had a p value of 0.41.

rows.group: The group that drank caffeinated coffee
The group that drank decaffeinated coffee

stimuli.text: Researchers investigated whether children imitate aggressive behavior that they observe. They recruited 72 preschool children and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Children in one condition watched a video of an adult hitting an inflatable doll. Children in the other condition watched a video of an adult playing quietly with other toys. The researchers then recorded the number of times that each child hit the doll during ten minutes of free play.

Researchers investigated whether nausea after a new taste produces an aversion to that taste. They recruited 40 laboratory rats and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Rats in one condition drank sweetened water and were then given an injection that causes mild nausea. Rats in the other condition drank sweetened water and were then given a harmless salt-water injection. The researchers then recorded the volume in milliliters of sweetened water that each rat drank the next day.

Researchers investigated whether the presence of other people slows the reporting of an emergency. They recruited 80 university students and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Participants in one condition were filling in a form in a room with four other people when smoke began to enter the room. Participants in the other condition were filling in the form alone when smoke began to enter the room. The researchers then recorded the time in seconds before each participant left the room to report the smoke.

Researchers investigated whether the color of a drink affects the ability to identify its flavor. They recruited 70 adult volunteers and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Participants in one condition tasted ten fruit drinks whose colors did not match their flavors. Participants in the other condition tasted the same ten drinks with matching colors. The researchers then recorded the number of flavors out of ten that each participant named correctly.

Read the summary of a hypothetical study, then answer parts A to F.

**Introduction.** Researchers investigated whether an expected reward reduces children's later interest in drawing. They hypothesized that an expected reward would affect intrinsic motivation to draw.

**Participants.** The sample was 60 preschool children who enjoyed drawing, recruited from one city. Parents gave informed consent, each child gave assent, and the plan was approved by an institutional review board. Families could withdraw at any time.

**Method.** The children were randomly assigned to one of two conditions. Children in one condition were promised a certificate for drawing and received it. Children in the other condition drew with no reward mentioned. The researchers recorded the number of minutes that each child chose to spend drawing during free time one week later.

**Results.** The group that was promised a certificate: mean minutes spent drawing = 6.5. The group that drew without a reward: mean minutes spent drawing = 13.8. The difference was statistically significant (p = 0.01).

Use the three hypothetical sources to answer the question: **Do rewards increase motivation?**

**Source A.** In an experiment, 60 preschool children who liked drawing were randomly assigned to draw for a promised certificate or to draw with no reward. A week later, during free play, the rewarded children chose to draw for a mean of 6.5 minutes and the unrewarded children for 13.8 minutes (p = 0.01).

**Source B.** In a study of 200 call-center workers, half were randomly assigned to receive a bonus for each sale. Over a month, the bonus group made a mean of 41 sales and the comparison group a mean of 33 (p = 0.02). When the bonus ended, the bonus group's sales fell to a mean of 30.

**Source C.** A survey of 500 university students found that students who said they studied mainly because they found their subject interesting had higher grades and reported less burnout than students who said they studied mainly for grades or money (r = +0.40 between interest and grades).

questions.stem: After months of unpaid bills and threats of eviction, Paul cannot sleep or concentrate. Which kind of stress is this?

options.why: The tend-and-befriend response is the response to stress of caring for others and seeking social support.
Eustress is the positive, motivating stress that comes from a challenge.
Correct. Distress is the negative stress that harms well-being and performance.
A stressor is an event or situation that a person sees as threatening or challenging.

questions.explanation: Distress is the negative stress that harms well-being and performance.

questions.stem: In a photo, two identical cars appear, and the one that looks smaller is judged to be farther away. Which depth cue is this?

options.why: Correct. Relative size is the monocular depth cue in which the object that casts the smaller image is seen as farther away.
Relative clarity is the monocular depth cue in which hazy objects are seen as farther away than sharp ones.
Retinal disparity is the binocular depth cue based on the difference between the images in the two eyes.
Linear perspective is the monocular depth cue in which parallel lines seem to meet in the distance.

questions.explanation: Relative size is the monocular depth cue in which the object that casts the smaller image is seen as farther away.

questions.stem: Four studies of child development report these correlation coefficients: +0.12, +0.28, +0.20, −0.52. Which coefficient shows the strongest relationship?

options.why: +0.20 is closer to zero.
+0.12 is closer to zero.
+0.28 is closer to zero.
Correct. Strength is the distance from zero, whatever the sign; −0.52 is farthest from zero.

questions.explanation: The sign of a correlation shows its direction; its distance from zero shows its strength. −0.52 is farthest from zero.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as any drug that acts on the brain to treat the symptoms of a psychological disorder?

options.why: Transcranial magnetic stimulation is the treatment in which repeated magnetic pulses are applied to the surface of the brain to treat depression.
Electroconvulsive therapy is the treatment for severe depression in which a brief electric current is passed through the brain of an anesthetized patient.
Correct. Psychotropic medication is any drug that acts on the brain to treat the symptoms of a psychological disorder.
A lobotomy is the now-abandoned form of psychosurgery that cut the nerves connecting the frontal lobes to the rest of the brain.

questions.explanation: Psychotropic medication is any drug that acts on the brain to treat the symptoms of a psychological disorder.

questions.stem: Bored on a quiet afternoon, Raj goes looking for something exciting to do, although all his physical needs are met. Which theory of motivation best explains this?

options.why: Homeostasis is the body's tendency to keep its internal state, such as temperature, steady.
Drive-reduction theory is the theory that a physical need creates a state of tension that motivates behavior to reduce it.
Incentive theory is the theory that behavior is pulled by rewards from outside the person.
Correct. Arousal theory is the theory that people are motivated to keep an ideal level of alertness and stimulation.

questions.explanation: Arousal theory is the theory that people are motivated to keep an ideal level of alertness and stimulation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as learning that takes place without reinforcement and is not shown until there is a reason to show it?

options.why: Correct. Latent learning is learning that takes place without reinforcement and is not shown until there is a reason to show it.
Modeling is the process of demonstrating a behavior that others then observe and imitate.
A cognitive map is a mental picture of the layout of one's surroundings.
Insight learning is the sudden realization of the solution to a problem.

questions.explanation: Latent learning is learning that takes place without reinforcement and is not shown until there is a reason to show it.

questions.stem: After being bitten by a large brown dog, Eva is afraid of all dogs. This best illustrates which of the following?

options.why: Spontaneous recovery is the reappearance of a weakened conditioned response after a rest period.
Stimulus discrimination is the learned ability to respond to the conditioned stimulus but not to similar stimuli.
Correct. Stimulus generalization is the tendency to respond to stimuli that are similar to the conditioned stimulus.
Acquisition is in classical conditioning, the first stage, in which the neutral stimulus is paired with the unconditioned stimulus and the response is learned.

questions.explanation: Stimulus generalization is the tendency to respond to stimuli that are similar to the conditioned stimulus.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes sampling bias?

options.text: A sample whose characteristics match those of the population it is drawn from
options.why: That describes a representative sample.

options.text: The extent to which the findings of a study apply to people beyond the sample
options.why: That describes generalizability.

options.text: A flaw in selecting participants that makes the sample unlike the population
options.why: Correct. This is what sampling bias means.

options.text: A sample made up of whoever is easiest for the researcher to reach
options.why: That describes a convenience sample.

questions.explanation: Sampling bias is a flaw in selecting participants that makes the sample unlike the population.

questions.stem: An elderly man increasingly forgets recent events, gets lost in familiar places and can no longer manage his money. Which term describes his condition?

options.why: The zone of proximal development is the gap between what a learner can do alone and what the learner can do with help.
Correct. Dementia is a serious decline in memory and thinking that interferes with daily life, most common in old age.
Crystallized intelligence is the accumulated knowledge and verbal skills that tend to increase with age.
Scaffolding is the temporary support that a more skilled person gives a learner and gradually removes.

questions.explanation: Dementia is a serious decline in memory and thinking that interferes with daily life, most common in old age.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as the arithmetic average of a set of scores?

options.why: Correct. The mean is the arithmetic average of a set of scores.
The mode is the score that occurs most often.
A positive skew is a distribution with a few extremely high scores, which pull the mean above the median.
The standard deviation is the measure of how much scores vary around the mean.

questions.explanation: The mean is the arithmetic average of a set of scores.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as the desire to do something to gain a reward or avoid a punishment?

options.why: An approach-avoidance conflict is a conflict in which one option has both attractive and unattractive features.
Correct. Extrinsic motivation is the desire to do something to gain a reward or avoid a punishment.
An approach-approach conflict is a conflict in which a person must choose between two attractive options.
Intrinsic motivation is the desire to do something for its own sake, because it is enjoyable or satisfying.

questions.explanation: Extrinsic motivation is the desire to do something to gain a reward or avoid a punishment.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as the part of working memory that briefly holds spoken and written words?

options.why: The visuospatial sketchpad is the part of working memory that briefly holds images and spatial information.
The central executive is the part of working memory that directs attention and coordinates the other parts.
Correct. The phonological loop is the part of working memory that briefly holds spoken and written words.
Long-term potentiation is the strengthening of the connections between neurons after repeated activation, which is the biological basis of memory.

questions.explanation: The phonological loop is the part of working memory that briefly holds spoken and written words.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes adverse childhood experiences?

options.text: The belief of adolescents that everyone is watching and judging them
options.why: That describes the imaginary audience.

options.text: The stressful or traumatic events in childhood, such as abuse or neglect, that raise the risk of later problems
options.why: Correct. This is what adverse childhood experiences means.

options.text: The period from about 18 to the mid-twenties, between adolescence and full independence
options.why: That describes emerging adulthood.

options.text: The play in which children act out imaginary roles and situations
options.why: That describes pretend play.

questions.explanation: Adverse childhood experiences is the stressful or traumatic events in childhood, such as abuse or neglect, that raise the risk of later problems.

questions.stem: A psychologist notes that people who score high on verbal tests also tend to score high on spatial and numerical tests, and concludes that one ability underlies them all. Which idea is this?

options.why: Mental age is the level of performance typical of a certain chronological age on an intelligence test.
Correct. General intelligence is the single underlying mental ability that Spearman believed affects performance on all mental tasks.
Multiple intelligences is the theory that people have several independent kinds of intelligence, such as musical and interpersonal.
The intelligence quotient is originally, mental age divided by chronological age and multiplied by 100.

questions.explanation: General intelligence is the single underlying mental ability that Spearman believed affects performance on all mental tasks.

questions.stem: Which of the following would be a confounding variable in this study?

options.text: Each one was assigned to a condition at random
options.why: Random assignment reduces confounding; it is not a confound.

options.text: The group holding the pen between the teeth saw the cartoons in color, and the other group saw them in black and white
options.why: Correct. It differs between the groups along with the independent variable, so it could explain the results instead.

options.text: The two groups differed in amusement at the end of the study
options.why: That is the dependent variable, the result being measured.

options.text: One group differed from the other in the facial expression produced by holding a pen
options.why: That is the independent variable itself.

questions.explanation: It differs between the groups along with the independent variable, so it could explain the results instead.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as the strategy of getting agreement to a small request first so that a larger request is more likely to be accepted?

options.why: A social norm is a rule for accepted and expected behavior in a group.
Informational social influence is the influence that comes from a person's willingness to accept others' views as evidence about reality.
Normative social influence is the influence that comes from a person's desire to gain approval or avoid rejection.
Correct. The foot-in-the-door technique is the strategy of getting agreement to a small request first so that a larger request is more likely to be accepted.

questions.explanation: The foot-in-the-door technique is the strategy of getting agreement to a small request first so that a larger request is more likely to be accepted.

questions.stem: Leah is sure a fact is true but cannot remember whether she read it in a textbook or saw it in a film. This best illustrates which of the following?

options.why: Constructive memory is the building of a memory at retrieval from stored pieces, expectations and later information.
The misinformation effect is the distortion of a memory by misleading information received after the event.
Correct. Source amnesia is the inability to remember where, when or how a piece of information was learned.
Imagination inflation is the increased confidence that an event happened after repeatedly imagining it.

questions.explanation: Source amnesia is the inability to remember where, when or how a piece of information was learned.

questions.stem: A depressed client believes she is worthless, that the world is unfair and that nothing will ever improve. This pattern is called which of the following?

options.why: Dialectical behavior therapy is the therapy that teaches skills for tolerating distress and controlling emotions, often used for borderline personality disorder.
Rational emotive behavior therapy is the confrontational cognitive therapy, developed by Ellis, that actively challenges a client's irrational beliefs.
Correct. The cognitive triad is the pattern of negative thoughts about oneself, the world and the future that is found in depression.
Cognitive-behavioral therapy is the therapy that combines changing self-defeating thoughts with changing behavior.

questions.explanation: The cognitive triad is the pattern of negative thoughts about oneself, the world and the future that is found in depression.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as the movement, begun in the 1950s, of patients out of psychiatric hospitals and into community care?

options.why: Evidence-based practice is the choosing of treatments on the basis of research, clinical skill and the client's own values.
The therapeutic alliance is the bond of trust and cooperation between therapist and client.
A meta-analysis is a statistical procedure that combines the results of many studies to reach an overall conclusion.
Correct. Deinstitutionalization is the movement, begun in the 1950s, of patients out of psychiatric hospitals and into community care.

questions.explanation: Deinstitutionalization is the movement, begun in the 1950s, of patients out of psychiatric hospitals and into community care.

questions.stem: Which of the following would be a confounding variable in this study?

options.text: One group differed from the other in the treatment
options.why: That is the independent variable itself.

options.text: The two groups differed in the severity of depression at the end of the study
options.why: That is the dependent variable, the result being measured.

options.text: Only the therapy group was also allowed to take antidepressant medication
options.why: Correct. It differs between the groups along with the independent variable, so it could explain the results instead.

options.text: Each one was assigned to a condition at random
options.why: Random assignment reduces confounding; it is not a confound.

questions.explanation: It differs between the groups along with the independent variable, so it could explain the results instead.

questions.stem: Receptors in Tia's fingertip detect a pinprick, and a signal travels toward her spinal cord. Which cells carry this incoming signal?

options.why: Glial cells is the cells that support, nourish, insulate and protect neurons.
The reflex arc is the simple automatic pathway in which the spinal cord produces a response before the brain is aware of the stimulus.
Correct. Sensory neurons is the neurons that carry incoming information from the sense receptors to the brain and spinal cord.
Motor neurons is the neurons that carry outgoing information from the brain and spinal cord to the muscles and glands.

questions.explanation: Sensory neurons is the neurons that carry incoming information from the sense receptors to the brain and spinal cord.

questions.stem: To treat severe epilepsy, surgeons cut the fibers that carry messages between the left and right hemispheres. Which structure was cut?

options.why: The amygdala is the structure that processes fear and aggression.
The cerebral cortex is the wrinkled outer layer of the brain, which handles thinking, perception and voluntary movement.
The hypothalamus is the structure that regulates hunger, thirst, body temperature and sexual behavior and controls the pituitary gland.
Correct. The corpus callosum is the band of fibers that connects the two hemispheres of the brain.

questions.explanation: The corpus callosum is the band of fibers that connects the two hemispheres of the brain.

questions.stem: After the study, the researchers explained its full purpose to every participant and answered their questions. What is this called?

options.why: Correct. Debriefing explains the study, including any deception, once it is over.
Replication is repeating a study.
Consent is obtained before the study.
A placebo is an inactive treatment.

questions.explanation: Debriefing explains the study, including any deception, once it is over.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as the eating disorder in which a person restricts food to the point of being dangerously underweight, with an intense fear of gaining weight?

options.why: Correct. Anorexia nervosa is the eating disorder in which a person restricts food to the point of being dangerously underweight, with an intense fear of gaining weight.
Binge-eating disorder is the eating disorder in which a person repeatedly eats very large amounts and feels distress, without purging afterward.
Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder is the neurodevelopmental disorder marked by inattention, hyperactivity and impulsiveness.
Autism spectrum disorder is the neurodevelopmental disorder marked by difficulties with social communication and by repetitive behaviors or narrow interests.

questions.explanation: Anorexia nervosa is the eating disorder in which a person restricts food to the point of being dangerously underweight, with an intense fear of gaining weight.

questions.stem: A doctor prescribes a drug that blocks dopamine receptors to reduce a patient's hallucinations. Which kind of drug is this?

options.why: Tardive dyskinesia is the involuntary movements of the face and tongue that can result from long-term use of antipsychotic drugs.
Correct. An antipsychotic drug is a drug that reduces hallucinations and delusions by blocking dopamine receptors.
An antidepressant is a drug, such as an SSRI, that treats depression and anxiety by raising the availability of serotonin or norepinephrine.
Lithium is the mood-stabilizing drug used to treat bipolar disorder.

questions.explanation: An antipsychotic drug is a drug that reduces hallucinations and delusions by blocking dopamine receptors.

questions.stem: Asked to describe herself, Kim lists that she is a daughter, an athlete, friendly and good at math. Together, these ideas form which of the following?

options.why: Reciprocal determinism is the idea that a person's behavior, thoughts and environment all influence one another.
Factor analysis is the statistical method that finds clusters of related test items, used to identify basic traits.
Correct. Self-concept is all the thoughts and feelings a person has in answer to the question 'Who am I?'.
Self-esteem is a person's overall feeling of self-worth.

questions.explanation: Self-concept is all the thoughts and feelings a person has in answer to the question 'Who am I?'.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as the condition in which the two hemispheres cannot communicate because the corpus callosum has been cut?

options.why: A case study is an in-depth study of one individual, such as a patient with unusual brain damage.
Correct. A split brain is the condition in which the two hemispheres cannot communicate because the corpus callosum has been cut.
An EEG is a recording of the electrical waves that sweep across the brain's surface.
Lesioning is the destruction of a small area of brain tissue to study its function.

questions.explanation: A split brain is the condition in which the two hemispheres cannot communicate because the corpus callosum has been cut.

questions.stem: Too little of one neurotransmitter is linked to the tremors of Parkinson's disease, and too much activity of it is linked to schizophrenia. Which neurotransmitter is this?

options.why: Norepinephrine is the neurotransmitter that helps control alertness and arousal.
Endorphins is the neurotransmitters that reduce pain and increase pleasure.
Correct. Dopamine is the neurotransmitter that influences movement, attention, and feelings of reward.
Serotonin is the neurotransmitter that affects mood, hunger and sleep.

questions.explanation: Dopamine is the neurotransmitter that influences movement, attention, and feelings of reward.

questions.stem: A child realizes that water poured from a short glass into a tall one could be poured back to give the same level as before. Which concept does this show?

options.why: Object permanence is the understanding that things continue to exist when they are out of sight.
Theory of mind is the understanding that other people have their own thoughts, beliefs and feelings.
Conservation is the understanding that quantity stays the same when shape or arrangement changes.
Correct. Reversibility is the understanding that an action can be undone to return things to their original state.

questions.explanation: Reversibility is the understanding that an action can be undone to return things to their original state.

questions.stem: Can the researchers conclude that intelligence test score at age 11 causes a change in average school grade at age 16?

options.text: Yes, because the sample was large
options.why: A large sample does not turn a correlation into evidence of causation.

options.text: No, because correlations can only be calculated in experiments
options.why: Correlations are calculated in non-experimental studies.

options.text: Yes, because the correlation is not zero
options.why: Any nonzero correlation still leaves the cause unknown.

options.text: No, because a correlation does not show cause and effect
options.why: Correct. Without manipulating a variable and assigning subjects at random, other explanations cannot be ruled out.

questions.explanation: Without manipulating a variable and assigning subjects at random, other explanations cannot be ruled out.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes amplitude?

options.text: The height of a sound wave, which determines loudness
options.why: Correct. This is what amplitude means.

options.text: The coiled, fluid-filled tube in the inner ear where sound waves become neural impulses
options.why: That describes the cochlea.

options.text: The number of sound waves per second, which determines pitch
options.why: That describes frequency.

options.text: The distance from one wave peak to the next, which determines the hue of light
options.why: That describes wavelength.

questions.explanation: Amplitude is the height of a sound wave, which determines loudness.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as an explanation of behavior that points to the person's own traits or character?

options.why: Correct. A dispositional attribution is an explanation of behavior that points to the person's own traits or character.
Downward social comparison is the comparing of oneself with people who are doing worse.
The mere exposure effect is the tendency to like something more simply because we have encountered it repeatedly.
A situational attribution is an explanation of behavior that points to outside circumstances.

questions.explanation: A dispositional attribution is an explanation of behavior that points to the person's own traits or character.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as the research method of collecting self-reported attitudes or behaviors from a sample by asking questions?

options.why: An operational definition is a statement of exactly how a variable is measured or manipulated in a study.
Correct. A survey is the research method of collecting self-reported attitudes or behaviors from a sample by asking questions.
Replication is the repeating of a study with different participants to see whether the finding holds.
An experiment is the research method in which a researcher manipulates a variable and randomly assigns participants, which allows conclusions about cause and effect.

questions.explanation: A survey is the research method of collecting self-reported attitudes or behaviors from a sample by asking questions.

questions.stem: After the study, the researchers explained its full purpose to every participant and answered their questions. What is this called?

options.why: Consent is obtained before the study.
A placebo is an inactive treatment.
Correct. Debriefing explains the study, including any deception, once it is over.
Replication is repeating a study.

questions.explanation: Debriefing explains the study, including any deception, once it is over.

questions.stem: In one culture, people are expected to hide their disappointment in public; in another, they show it openly. This difference reflects which of the following?

options.why: The broaden-and-build theory is the theory that positive emotions widen a person's awareness and help build lasting skills and resources.
Correct. A display rule is a cultural rule about which emotions may be shown, when and to whom.
The facial-feedback hypothesis is the idea that the expression on a person's face can influence the emotion the person feels.
An elicitor is an event or stimulus that triggers an emotion.

questions.explanation: A display rule is a cultural rule about which emotions may be shown, when and to whom.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes in-group bias?

options.text: The discomfort a person feels when their actions and attitudes conflict, which motivates a change in one of them
options.why: That describes cognitive dissonance.

options.text: The tendency to see the members of other groups as all alike
options.why: That describes out-group homogeneity bias.

options.text: The tendency to favor the members of one's own group
options.why: Correct. This is what in-group bias means.

options.text: The tendency to search for and favor information that supports what one already believes
options.why: That describes confirmation bias.

questions.explanation: In-group bias is the tendency to favor the members of one's own group.

questions.stem: After two years of long hours and constant pressure, a nurse feels drained, detached and ineffective. This best illustrates which of the following?

options.why: An industrial-organizational psychologist is a psychologist who studies behavior in the workplace to improve productivity and well-being.
Altruism is unselfish concern for the welfare of others.
Correct. Burnout is the physical and emotional exhaustion that results from long-term stress at work.
The bystander effect is the tendency for a person to be less likely to help when other people are present.

questions.explanation: Burnout is the physical and emotional exhaustion that results from long-term stress at work.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes obedience?

options.text: The following of the direct commands of an authority figure
options.why: Correct. This is what obedience means.

options.text: The view that the different cultural groups in a society should be valued and should keep their identities
options.why: That describes multiculturalism.

options.text: A situation in which people who each pursue their own interest end up harming everyone
options.why: That describes a social trap.

options.text: The tendency to overestimate how many other people share our opinions and behaviors
options.why: That describes the false consensus effect.

questions.explanation: Obedience is the following of the direct commands of an authority figure.

questions.stem: The smell of sunscreen instantly brings back a vivid memory of a childhood holiday. Which sense has this close link to emotion and memory areas?

options.why: A pheromone is a chemical signal released by one member of a species that affects the behavior of others.
Gustation is the sense of taste, which detects sweet, sour, salty, bitter, umami and oleogustus.
Correct. Olfaction is the sense of smell, the only sense that does not pass through the thalamus first.
A supertaster is a person with more taste receptors than average, who experiences tastes more intensely.

questions.explanation: Olfaction is the sense of smell, the only sense that does not pass through the thalamus first.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as a step-by-step procedure that guarantees a solution?

options.why: Divergent thinking is thinking that produces many possible answers to a problem.
Functional fixedness is the inability to see that an object can be used for something other than its usual purpose.
A mental set is the tendency to approach a problem in a way that has worked before, even when it no longer works.
Correct. An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure that guarantees a solution.

questions.explanation: An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure that guarantees a solution.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes a morpheme?

options.text: The smallest unit of language that carries meaning
options.why: Correct. This is what a morpheme means.

options.text: The rules for ordering words into sentences
options.why: That describes syntax.

options.text: The rules by which we get meaning from words and sentences
options.why: That describes semantics.

options.text: The smallest distinctive unit of sound in a language
options.why: That describes a phoneme.

questions.explanation: A morpheme is the smallest unit of language that carries meaning.

questions.stem: Raccoons trained to drop coins into a box began rubbing the coins together as if washing food, despite getting no reward for it. This best illustrates which of the following?

options.why: Superstitious behavior is a behavior that is repeated because it happened by chance just before a reward.
Learned helplessness is the passive giving up that follows repeated experiences of being unable to avoid bad events.
Correct. Instinctive drift is the tendency of a trained animal to return to its natural, inborn behaviors.
A primary reinforcer is a reinforcer, such as food or water, that satisfies a biological need and is rewarding without learning.

questions.explanation: Instinctive drift is the tendency of a trained animal to return to its natural, inborn behaviors.

questions.stem: Freud argued that slips of the tongue reveal wishes that people do not know they have. Where did he believe these wishes are held?

options.why: The self-actualizing tendency is in humanistic theory, the inborn drive of people to grow and fulfill their potential.
A projective test is a personality test, such as an inkblot test, that asks people to interpret unclear images in order to reveal hidden feelings.
Correct. The unconscious is in psychodynamic theory, the store of thoughts, wishes and memories that a person is not aware of but that still influences behavior.
Unconditional positive regard is the attitude of total acceptance toward another person, whatever they say or do.

questions.explanation: The unconscious is in psychodynamic theory, the store of thoughts, wishes and memories that a person is not aware of but that still influences behavior.

questions.stem: On the way home, Lin remembers that she must stop to buy milk. Which kind of memory is this?

options.why: Correct. Prospective memory is the memory to carry out a planned action in the future.
Procedural memory is the implicit memory of how to perform skills and actions.
Semantic memory is the explicit memory of facts and general knowledge.
Episodic memory is the explicit memory of personally experienced events.

questions.explanation: Prospective memory is the memory to carry out a planned action in the future.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the operational definition of the dependent variable?

options.text: The number of words out of 40 that each participant recalled on a test one month later
options.why: Correct. An operational definition states exactly how a variable is measured.
This is the independent variable.

options.text: The random assignment of each one to a condition
options.why: This is a control procedure, not a definition of a variable.
This names the variable but does not say how it was measured.

questions.explanation: An operational definition states exactly how a variable is measured.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a possible third variable that could explain the correlation?

options.text: The warmth of parenting, as rated by observers
options.why: This is one of the two variables that were measured.
This is the statistic, not a variable.
This is one of the two variables that were measured.

options.text: The level of financial stress in the family
options.why: Correct. A third variable could influence both measures and so produce the correlation.

questions.explanation: A third variable could influence both measures and so produce the correlation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as the developmental question of which traits stay the same through life and which ones alter?

options.why: Nature and nurture is the developmental question of how heredity and experience together shape a person.
A longitudinal study is research that follows the same people and retests them over a long period.
A cross-sectional study is research that compares people of different ages at one point in time.
Correct. Stability and change is the developmental question of which traits stay the same through life and which ones alter.

questions.explanation: Stability and change is the developmental question of which traits stay the same through life and which ones alter.

questions.stem: Paul cannot make even small decisions without reassurance and will do anything to keep others looking after him. Which disorder does this suggest?

options.why: Correct. Dependent personality disorder is the personality disorder marked by an excessive need to be taken care of and by clinging, submissive behavior.
Paranoid personality disorder is the personality disorder marked by lasting distrust and suspicion of others.
Antisocial personality disorder is the personality disorder marked by a lack of conscience and disregard for the rights of others.
Narcissistic personality disorder is the personality disorder marked by an exaggerated sense of self-importance and a need for admiration.

questions.explanation: Dependent personality disorder is the personality disorder marked by an excessive need to be taken care of and by clinging, submissive behavior.

questions.stem: A psychologist says a client's phobia was learned when a dog bite was paired with fear, and is kept going because avoiding dogs brings relief. Which perspective is this?

options.why: The cognitive perspective is the view that disorders result from distorted or irrational ways of thinking.
The psychodynamic perspective is the view that disorders result from unconscious conflicts, often rooted in childhood.
Correct. The behavioral perspective is the view that disorders result from learned associations and reinforcement.
The sociocultural perspective is the view that disorders result from social and cultural factors, such as poverty and discrimination.

questions.explanation: The behavioral perspective is the view that disorders result from learned associations and reinforcement.

questions.stem: After an infection damaged the tiny bones of his middle ear, Arun's hearing was restored with a hearing aid that amplifies sound. Which kind of hearing loss did he have?

options.why: Frequency theory is the theory that we hear pitch because the rate of nerve impulses matches the frequency of the sound.
Correct. Conduction deafness is hearing loss caused by damage to the eardrum or the bones of the middle ear.
Place theory is the theory that we hear different pitches because different sound waves trigger different places on the cochlea's membrane.
Sensorineural deafness is hearing loss caused by damage to the hair cells of the cochlea or to the auditory nerve.

questions.explanation: Conduction deafness is hearing loss caused by damage to the eardrum or the bones of the middle ear.

questions.stem: Zoe is taking classes in art, biology and law to work out what she wants, and she has not decided yet. Which identity status is this?

options.why: Identity diffusion is the identity status of a person who has neither explored options nor made a commitment.
Identity foreclosure is the identity status of a person who has made a commitment without exploring options.
Correct. Identity moratorium is the identity status of a person who is actively exploring options but has not yet made a commitment.
Identity achievement is the identity status of a person who has explored options and made a commitment.

questions.explanation: Identity moratorium is the identity status of a person who is actively exploring options but has not yet made a commitment.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as the therapy in which several clients meet together with a therapist and benefit from each other's support?

options.why: Dream interpretation is the psychodynamic technique of analyzing dreams to uncover unconscious wishes and conflicts.
Active listening is the technique of echoing, restating and seeking clarification of what the client says.
Correct. Group therapy is the therapy in which several clients meet together with a therapist and benefit from each other's support.
Hypnosis is a state of heightened suggestibility that can help reduce pain and anxiety but does not reliably recover memories.

questions.explanation: Group therapy is the therapy in which several clients meet together with a therapist and benefit from each other's support.

questions.stem: Which statement about the results is best supported?

options.text: The difference between the groups is statistically significant, so it is unlikely to be due to chance
options.why: Correct. A p value below 0.05 means a difference this large would rarely occur by chance alone.

options.text: The results prove that every individual in the first group differed from every individual in the second
options.why: The table reports group averages, not individual scores.

options.text: The two groups had the same average result
options.why: The table shows different averages.

options.text: The difference between the groups is probably due to chance
options.why: A p value of 0.01 is below 0.05, so chance is an unlikely explanation.

questions.explanation: A p value below 0.05 means a difference this large would rarely occur by chance alone.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as perception that is guided by experience, expectations and context?

options.why: The cocktail party effect is the ability to notice personally important information, such as your name, in an unattended conversation.
A perceptual set is a readiness to perceive something in a particular way because of expectations.
Selective attention is the focusing of awareness on one stimulus while ignoring others.
Correct. Top-down processing is perception that is guided by experience, expectations and context.

questions.explanation: Top-down processing is perception that is guided by experience, expectations and context.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes trust versus mistrust?

options.text: Erikson's stage in infancy, in which babies learn whether their needs will be met
options.why: Correct. This is what trust versus mistrust means.

options.text: Erikson's stage in the preschool years, in which children learn to start tasks and carry out plans
options.why: That describes initiative versus guilt.

options.text: Erikson's stage in toddlerhood, in which children learn to do things for themselves
options.why: That describes autonomy versus shame and doubt.

options.text: Erikson's stage in elementary school, in which children learn to feel competent or else feel inadequate
options.why: That describes industry versus inferiority.

questions.explanation: Trust versus mistrust is Erikson's stage in infancy, in which babies learn whether their needs will be met.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as the need for larger doses of a drug to get the same effect after repeated use?

options.why: Withdrawal is the unpleasant physical and psychological symptoms that follow stopping an addictive drug.
A reuptake inhibitor is a drug that keeps a neurotransmitter in the synapse longer by blocking its reabsorption.
An agonist is a drug that increases the action of a neurotransmitter, for example by mimicking it.
Correct. Tolerance is the need for larger doses of a drug to get the same effect after repeated use.

questions.explanation: Tolerance is the need for larger doses of a drug to get the same effect after repeated use.

questions.stem: What is the dependent variable in this study?

options.why: A hypothesis is a prediction, not a variable.

options.text: The condition to which each one was assigned
options.why: This describes the independent variable.
Correct. The dependent variable is the outcome that the researchers measured.
This was manipulated by the researchers: it is the independent variable.

questions.explanation: The dependent variable is the outcome that the researchers measured.

questions.stem: A therapist refuses to exaggerate her qualifications or to make false claims about how well a treatment works. Which ethical principle is she following?

options.text: Respect for people's rights and dignity
options.why: Respect for people's rights and dignity is the ethical principle that psychologists must protect privacy, confidentiality and the right of people to make their own choices.
Fidelity is the ethical principle that psychologists must be trustworthy and keep their professional promises.
Nonmaleficence is the ethical principle that psychologists must avoid doing harm.
Correct. Integrity is the ethical principle that psychologists must be honest and accurate.

questions.explanation: Integrity is the ethical principle that psychologists must be honest and accurate.

questions.stem: Sam is warm, quick to forgive and always willing to help. He would score high on which Big Five trait?

options.why: Openness to experience is the Big Five trait of being imaginative, curious and willing to try new things.
Extraversion is the Big Five trait of being sociable, outgoing and energetic.
Emotional stability is the Big Five trait of being calm and secure rather than anxious and moody.
Correct. Agreeableness is the Big Five trait of being kind, trusting and cooperative.

questions.explanation: Agreeableness is the Big Five trait of being kind, trusting and cooperative.

questions.stem: A second study of a different pair of measures finds r = −0.55. Which relationship is stronger?

options.text: The relationship with the positive sign, whatever its size
options.why: The sign shows direction, not strength.

options.text: The relationship in the first study, because its coefficient is closer to zero
options.why: A coefficient closer to zero shows a weaker relationship.

options.text: The relationship in the second study, because its coefficient is farther from zero
options.why: Correct. The strength of a correlation is its distance from zero, whatever the sign.

options.text: Neither, because relationships with different signs cannot be compared
options.why: Strength can be compared by distance from zero.

questions.explanation: The strength of a correlation is its distance from zero, whatever the sign.

questions.stem: A day after meeting twelve new people, Joy remembers only the names of the first two she met. This best illustrates which of the following?

options.why: The recency effect is the tendency to remember the last items in a list well.
The spacing effect is the finding that study spread over time produces better long-term memory than study crammed together.
Correct. The primacy effect is the tendency to remember the first items in a list well.
The serial position effect is the tendency to remember the first and last items in a list better than the middle ones.

questions.explanation: The primacy effect is the tendency to remember the first items in a list well.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes a compulsion?

options.text: A repeated action that a person feels driven to perform to reduce anxiety
options.why: Correct. This is what a compulsion means.

options.text: The disorder in which a person has flashbacks, nightmares, watchfulness and avoidance for more than a month after a terrifying event
options.why: That describes posttraumatic stress disorder.

options.text: The disorder in which a person shows two or more distinct personalities that take control at different times
options.why: That describes dissociative identity disorder.

options.text: An unwanted thought or urge that keeps returning and causes anxiety
options.why: That describes an obsession.

questions.explanation: A compulsion is a repeated action that a person feels driven to perform to reduce anxiety.

questions.stem: Which statement about the results is best supported?

options.text: The study shows that the two conditions always give identical results
options.why: A non-significant result does not show that there is no effect at all.

options.text: The independent variable had a large effect
options.why: The averages are close and the difference is not significant.

options.text: The difference between the groups is statistically significant
options.why: A p value of 0.41 is far above 0.05.

options.text: The difference between the groups is not statistically significant, so it could easily be due to chance
options.why: Correct. A p value above 0.05 means a difference this size would often occur by chance alone.

questions.explanation: A p value above 0.05 means a difference this size would often occur by chance alone.

questions.stem: After many months of unrelieved stress, Lia feels worn out and catches one infection after another. Which phase of the general adaptation syndrome is this?

options.why: The general adaptation syndrome is Selye's three-phase description of the body's response to long-term stress: alarm, resistance and exhaustion.
The resistance phase is the second phase of the general adaptation syndrome, in which the body stays highly aroused to cope with a continuing stressor.
Correct. The exhaustion phase is the third phase of the general adaptation syndrome, in which the body's resources run out and illness becomes more likely.
The alarm reaction is the first phase of the general adaptation syndrome, in which the sympathetic nervous system is suddenly activated.

questions.explanation: The exhaustion phase is the third phase of the general adaptation syndrome, in which the body's resources run out and illness becomes more likely.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes resilience?

options.text: The positive character traits, such as kindness or curiosity, that are most central to a particular person
options.why: That describes signature strengths.

options.text: The scientific study of the strengths and conditions that help people and communities thrive
options.why: That describes positive psychology.

options.text: The ability to recover and adapt well after stress or hardship
options.why: Correct. This is what resilience means.

options.text: The positive psychological change that some people experience after struggling with a very difficult event
options.why: That describes posttraumatic growth.

questions.explanation: Resilience is the ability to recover and adapt well after stress or hardship.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the operational definition of the dependent variable?

options.text: The behavior of an adult model
options.why: This is the independent variable.
This names the variable but does not say how it was measured.

options.text: The random assignment of each one to a condition
options.why: This is a control procedure, not a definition of a variable.

options.text: The number of times that each child hit the doll during ten minutes of free play
options.why: Correct. An operational definition states exactly how a variable is measured.

questions.explanation: An operational definition states exactly how a variable is measured.

questions.stem: Severe stress early in life switches off a gene in a rat pup, even though the pup's DNA sequence is unchanged. Which field studies this kind of effect?

options.why: An adoption study is research that compares adopted children with their biological and adoptive relatives.
Nature is the influence of inherited genetic factors on behavior and mental processes.
Correct. Epigenetics is the study of how the environment changes whether genes are expressed without changing the DNA itself.
Nurture is the influence of environmental factors, such as upbringing and experience, on behavior and mental processes.

questions.explanation: Epigenetics is the study of how the environment changes whether genes are expressed without changing the DNA itself.

questions.stem: A researcher claims that dreams help move the day's experiences into long-term storage. Which theory of dreaming is this?

options.why: Memory consolidation is the strengthening of memories that takes place during sleep.
The activation-synthesis theory is the theory that dreams are the brain's attempt to make sense of random neural activity during sleep.
Correct. The consolidation theory is the theory that dreaming helps sort and strengthen the day's memories.
Restoration is the repair of body and brain tissue that takes place during sleep.

questions.explanation: The consolidation theory is the theory that dreaming helps sort and strengthen the day's memories.

questions.stem: Which of the following would be a confounding variable in this study?

options.text: Each one was assigned to a condition at random
options.why: Random assignment reduces confounding; it is not a confound.

options.text: The rats given the nausea-causing injection were several months older
options.why: Correct. It differs between the groups along with the independent variable, so it could explain the results instead.

options.text: The two groups differed in preference for sweetened water at the end of the study
options.why: That is the dependent variable, the result being measured.

options.text: One group differed from the other in the type of injection given after drinking
options.why: That is the independent variable itself.

questions.explanation: It differs between the groups along with the independent variable, so it could explain the results instead.

questions.stem: As a friend walks away, her image on Tom's retina shrinks, but he does not think she is getting smaller. This best illustrates which of the following?

options.why: Color constancy is the perception that an object keeps the same color under different lighting.
Apparent movement is the perception of motion when a series of still images or lights is shown in quick succession.
Shape constancy is the perception that an object keeps the same shape even when the viewing angle changes.
Correct. Size constancy is the perception that an object keeps the same size even when its image on the retina changes.

questions.explanation: Size constancy is the perception that an object keeps the same size even when its image on the retina changes.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes working memory?

options.text: The relatively permanent and limitless store of knowledge, skills and experiences
options.why: That describes long-term memory.

options.text: The brief sensory memory of a visual image, which lasts a few tenths of a second
options.why: That describes iconic memory.

options.text: The sensory memory of a sound, which lasts three or four seconds
options.why: That describes echoic memory.

options.text: The active processing of information held in mind, combining new input with knowledge from long-term memory
options.why: Correct. This is what working memory means.

questions.explanation: Working memory is the active processing of information held in mind, combining new input with knowledge from long-term memory.

questions.stem: Which structure changes its curvature, in a process called accommodation, to focus near or far objects?

options.why: Rods is the receptor cells that detect black, white and gray and work in dim light and peripheral vision.
The fovea is the central point of the retina, where cones are packed most densely and vision is sharpest.
Correct. The lens is the transparent structure that changes shape to focus light on the retina.
The retina is the light-sensitive inner surface at the back of the eye that contains the receptor cells.

questions.explanation: The lens is the transparent structure that changes shape to focus light on the retina.

questions.stem: Scores on a test are normally distributed with a mean of 70 and a standard deviation of 10. About what percentage of scores are above 90?

options.why: Correct. 95% lie within two standard deviations, leaving 5% outside, half of which (2.5%) is above.
This does not match the 68–95 rule for a normal distribution.
This does not match the 68–95 rule for a normal distribution.
This does not match the 68–95 rule for a normal distribution.

questions.title: Article analysis: a study of intrinsic motivation to draw

parts.prompt: Identify the research method used in the study.

rubric.criterion: Identifies the method as an experiment.
rubric.example: The study is an experiment: the researchers manipulated a variable and randomly assigned the subjects to conditions.

parts.prompt: State the operational definition of intrinsic motivation to draw.

rubric.criterion: States how the variable was measured in this study.
rubric.example: Intrinsic motivation to draw was defined as the number of minutes that each child chose to spend drawing during free time one week later.

parts.prompt: Describe the meaning of the difference between the two group averages.

rubric.criterion: Accurately describes which group scored higher or lower and what that means for the variable measured.
rubric.example: The group that was promised a certificate later spent less time drawing. On average, the value was 6.5 for the group that was promised a certificate and 13.8 for the group that drew without a reward, and a p value of 0.01 means a difference this large is unlikely to be due to chance.

parts.prompt: Identify at least one ethical guideline applied by the researchers.

rubric.criterion: Identifies an ethical guideline that the summary shows was followed.
rubric.example: Informed consent and assent: parents consented and each child agreed to take part. (Also acceptable: approval by an institutional review board; the right to withdraw.)

parts.prompt: Explain the extent to which the research findings may or may not be generalizable, using specific and relevant evidence from the study.

rubric.criterion: Explains a limit (or strength) of generalizability with reference to the sample.
rubric.example: The sample was 60 preschool children who enjoyed drawing from one city, so the findings may not apply to people of other ages, cultures or backgrounds. Because the sample was not randomly selected from a wider population, it may not be representative.

parts.prompt: Explain how at least one of the research findings supports or refutes the researchers' hypothesis.

rubric.criterion: Uses a specific finding from the study as evidence.
rubric.example: The group that was promised a certificate later spent less time drawing. (6.5 compared with 13.8).

rubric.criterion: Explains how the finding supports the hypothesis, using a psychological concept.
rubric.example: This supports the hypothesis that an expected reward affects intrinsic motivation to draw. Because subjects were randomly assigned, the difference can be attributed to an expected reward. The finding illustrates intrinsic and extrinsic motivation: an external reward can reduce the desire to do an activity for its own sake.

questions.title: Evidence-based question: Do rewards increase motivation?

parts.prompt: Propose a specific and defensible claim, based in psychological science, that responds to the question.

rubric.criterion: States a claim that answers the question and can be supported by the sources.
rubric.example: Rewards increase a behavior while they last, but they can reduce intrinsic motivation, so the behavior falls when the rewards stop.

parts.prompt: (i) Support your claim using at least one piece of specific and relevant evidence from one of the sources. (ii) Explain how the evidence supports your claim, using a psychological perspective, theory, concept or research finding learned in AP Psychology.

rubric.criterion: Uses specific, relevant evidence from one source and names the source.
rubric.example: In Source A, children promised a certificate later chose to draw for 6.5 minutes, compared with 13.8 minutes for children who were not rewarded.

rubric.criterion: Explains how the evidence supports the claim.
rubric.example: This supports the claim through intrinsic and extrinsic motivation: the reward gave the children an external reason for drawing, which weakened their desire to draw for its own sake.

rubric.criterion: Correctly applies a psychological concept in the explanation.
rubric.example: The concept must be named and applied correctly, as in the model explanation.

parts.prompt: (i) Support your claim using an additional piece of specific and relevant evidence from a different source. (ii) Explain how this evidence supports your claim, using a different psychological perspective, theory, concept or research finding.

rubric.criterion: Uses specific, relevant evidence from a different source and names the source.
rubric.example: In Source B, workers paid a bonus made more sales (41 compared with 33), but their sales fell to 30 when the bonus ended.

rubric.criterion: Explains how the evidence supports the claim.
rubric.example: This supports the claim through operant conditioning: the bonus acted as positive reinforcement, which increased the behavior, and when reinforcement stopped the behavior declined (extinction).

rubric.criterion: Correctly applies a different psychological concept from the one used in part B.
rubric.example: The concept must differ from the one used in part B and be applied correctly.
